description: We are a team of ambitious students, who want to work hard and make something new and innovative.
summary:
EVA Sim is an astronaut helmet with a heads-up display projected on the inside of the visor. Built for the Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map challenge, it lets astronauts plan and rehearse a Mars spacewalk at Jezero Crater on real NASA terrain.

The display guides the astronaut through each task so they can work efficiently and use as few resources as possible. It also keeps them safe by tracking oxygen, temperature and calorie burn, and keeping those readings in view so they never have to look away from the job.

To make the demonstration realistic, we based the physics and the oxygen, temperature and calorie consumption rates on published data and research. We built it with Three.js, React and Electron, so it runs as a desktop app.

This matters because on Mars, oxygen and food are limited and help from Earth is minutes away. A helmet that keeps the astronaut informed and on task makes every spacewalk safer and more efficient.
details:
What it does
Sharkies: EVA Sim lets an astronaut plan and rehearse a spacewalk at Jezero Crater, where Perseverance landed, on real NASA/USGS HiRISE height data. You start inside the habitat. At the operations console you pick the tasks for the EVA and see the route on a topographic map. The console also shows how much oxygen the walk, the tasks and the reserve need, and the survival odds of the plan. Then you suit up at the airlock and walk out in first person.

Outside, everything you need is projected on the inside of the helmet visor: your objectives and time, oxygen, suit temperature and warnings. The display shows only what matters at that moment, so the view stays clear. When something goes wrong, like low oxygen, it warns you and tells you to head back to base, but the astronaut makes the decision.

At each stop you do science tasks based on Perseverance's real work: abrading a rock, drilling a core sample, leaving a sample tube at a depot and running a small MOXIE-style unit that makes oxygen from the Martian air.

How it works

  • Oxygen: every step costs oxygen based on your speed and the slope. Uphill costs more than downhill, and running costs more than walking. We convert workload into oxygen using NASA's Life Support Baseline Values (293 W of work uses 75 g of O₂ per hour) and Mars gravity of 3.71 m/s².
  • Calories: the energy cost per metre comes from a published walking-on-slopes curve (Minetti), adjusted for Mars gravity and the weight of the suit.
  • Temperature: a heat-balance model of the body, the air in the suit and the outer shell calculates the suit temperature as you work.
  • Route planning: a pathfinder (Dijkstra's algorithm) finds the route across the terrain that uses the least oxygen and the best order to visit the tasks. It always knows the cheapest way home from where you are standing.
  • Survival odds: the plan is run 1,000 times with random events like suit leaks, falls and dust devils. This shows how often the astronaut gets back with oxygen to spare.

Benefits and intended impact
On Mars, oxygen, food and time are limited, and Earth is too far away to help in an emergency. Sharkies helps astronauts get the most science done for the least oxygen and energy. It also gives them clear safety information without taking their eyes off the job. Rehearsing an EVA on the real terrain first means fewer surprises on the day. The same approach could be used for astronaut training, mission planning and showing the public what a Mars spacewalk really involves.

Tools and languages
TypeScript and React for the interface, Three.js for the 3D world and helmet, and Electron so it runs offline as a desktop app on Linux and Windows. We used Vite to build it and Python to prepare the terrain data. All the suit sounds are generated in code. It runs on an ordinary laptop, with no special hardware.

What makes it creative

  • The information isn't on a dashboard. It sits on the curved glass inside the helmet, where an astronaut would actually see it. The view through the bubble helmet bends slightly like real curved polycarbonate, and you can see the mic, drink tube and neck ring inside.
  • The sound is realistic. Mars air is very thin, so outside sounds are faint and you mostly hear your own breathing and life-support fan.
  • The tasks are based on real Perseverance operations, and the rocks on the ground are scattered the way they look in Perseverance's photos.

Factors we considered

  • Scientific honesty: every number is traced to a NASA source. Where we had to assume something, like suit mass, tank size or how often a leak happens, we labelled it as an assumption.
  • Human in the loop: the suit suggests and the astronaut decides.
  • Minimal display: too much on the visor is a distraction and a safety risk.
  • Working offline: a real Mars crew can't rely on the internet.
